claim: Condensin I is a pentameric protein complex that plays an essential role in mitotic chromosome assembly in eukaryotic cells.
source: Condensin I is a pentameric protein complex that plays an essential role in mitotic chromosome assembly in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about condensin I's structure and function.

claim: Condensin I loading is mitosis specific.
source: Although it has been shown that condensin I loading is mitosis specific, it remains poorly understood how the robust cell cycle regulation of condensin I is achieved.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Deletion of the N-tail accelerates condensin I loading in Xenopus egg mitotic extracts.
source: Deletion of the N-tail accelerates condensin I loading and chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg mitotic extracts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Deletion of the N-tail accelerates chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg mitotic extracts.
source: Deletion of the N-tail accelerates condensin I loading and chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg mitotic extracts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Phosphorylation-deficient mutations in the CAP-H N-tail decelerate condensin I loading.
source: Phosphorylation-deficient and phosphorylation-mimetic mutations in the CAP-H N-tail decelerate and accelerate condensin I loading, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Phosphorylation-mimetic mutations in the CAP-H N-tail accelerate condensin I loading.
source: Phosphorylation-deficient and phosphorylation-mimetic mutations in the CAP-H N-tail decelerate and accelerate condensin I loading, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Deletion of the N-tail enables condensin I to assemble mitotic chromosome-like structures even in interphase extracts.
source: Remarkably, deletion of the N-tail enables condensin I to assemble mitotic chromosome-like structures even in interphase extracts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Many eukaryotic species have two different condensin complexes, known as condensins I and II.
source: Many eukaryotic species have two different condensin complexes, known as condensins I and II, although some species including fungi have only condensin I.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of chromosome biology.

claim: Some species including fungi have only condensin I.
source: Many eukaryotic species have two different condensin complexes, known as condensins I and II, although some species including fungi have only condensin I.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of chromosome biology.

claim: The two condensin complexes share a pair of SMC ATPase subunits (SMC2 and SMC4).
source: The two condensin complexes, each of which is composed of five subunits, share a pair of SMC (structural maintenance of chromosome) ATPase subunits (SMC2 and SMC4) but are distinguished by distinct sets of non-SMC subunits (Ono et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ono et al., 2003.

claim: The two condensin complexes are distinguished by distinct sets of non-SMC subunits.
source: The two condensin complexes, each of which is composed of five subunits, share a pair of SMC (structural maintenance of chromosome) ATPase subunits (SMC2 and SMC4) but are distinguished by distinct sets of non-SMC subunits (Ono et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ono et al., 2003.

claim: In condensin I, the kleisin subunit CAP-H bridges the head domains of a V-shaped SMC2–SMC4 heterodimer.
source: In condensin I, the kleisin subunit CAP-H bridges the head domains of a V-shaped SMC2–SMC4 heterodimer, and is then bound by a pair of HEAT subunits, CAP-D2 and -G (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and established structural knowledge.

claim: CAP-H is bound by a pair of HEAT subunits, CAP-D2 and -G.
source: In condensin I, the kleisin subunit CAP-H bridges the head domains of a V-shaped SMC2–SMC4 heterodimer, and is then bound by a pair of HEAT subunits, CAP-D2 and -G (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and established structural knowledge.

claim: In vertebrates, the two condensin complexes cooperate to assemble rod-shaped chromosomes in mitosis.
source: In vertebrates, the two condensin complexes cooperate to assemble rod-shaped chromosomes in mitosis (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011; Green et al., 2012; Gibcus et al., 2018), but they display differential subcellular localization during the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Condensins I and II display differential subcellular localization during the cell cycle.
source: In vertebrates, the two condensin complexes cooperate to assemble rod-shaped chromosomes in mitosis (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011; Green et al., 2012; Gibcus et al., 2018), but they display differential subcellular localization during the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: In HeLa cells, condensin I primarily resides in the cytoplasm during interphase.
source: In HeLa cells, for instance, condensin I primarily resides in the cytoplasm during interphase, and gets loaded onto chromosomes immediately after the nuclear envelope breaks down in prometaphase (Ono et al., 2004; Hirota et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ono et al., 2004 and Hirota et al., 2004.

claim: In HeLa cells, condensin I gets loaded onto chromosomes immediately after the nuclear envelope breaks down in prometaphase.
source: In HeLa cells, for instance, condensin I primarily resides in the cytoplasm during interphase, and gets loaded onto chromosomes immediately after the nuclear envelope breaks down in prometaphase (Ono et al., 2004; Hirota et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ono et al., 2004 and Hirota et al., 2004.

claim: Mitosis-specific loading of condensin I can be recapitulated in membrane-free Xenopus egg extracts.
source: However, mitosis-specific loading of condensin I can be recapitulated in membrane-free Xenopus egg extracts (Hirano et al., 1997), suggesting that a mechanism(s) independent of the regulation of subcellular localization also operates to ensure the mitosis-specific action of condensin I.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hirano et al., 1997.

claim: A mechanism independent of the regulation of subcellular localization operates to ensure the mitosis-specific action of condensin I.
source: However, mitosis-specific loading of condensin I can be recapitulated in membrane-free Xenopus egg extracts (Hirano et al., 1997), suggesting that a mechanism(s) independent of the regulation of subcellular localization also operates to ensure the mitosis-specific action of condensin I.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mitosis-specific loading occurs in membrane-free extracts.

claim: The kleisin subunit CAP-H of condensin I has five sequence motifs widely conserved among eukaryotes.
source: The kleisin subunit CAP-H of condensin I has five sequence motifs widely conserved among eukaryotes (Figure 1A; Hara et al., 2019; Kinoshita et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Motif I of CAP-H binds to the SMC2 neck region.
source: Among them, motifs I and V bind to the SMC2 neck and the SMC4 cap regions, respectively (Hassler et al., 2019), whereas motifs II and IV interact with CAP-D2 and CAP-G, respectively (Piazza et al., 2014; Kschonsak et al., 2017; Hara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hassler et al., 2019.

claim: Motif V of CAP-H binds to the SMC4 cap region.
source: Among them, motifs I and V bind to the SMC2 neck and the SMC4 cap regions, respectively (Hassler et al., 2019), whereas motifs II and IV interact with CAP-D2 and CAP-G, respectively (Piazza et al., 2014; Kschonsak et al., 2017; Hara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hassler et al., 2019.

claim: Motif II of CAP-H interacts with CAP-D2.
source: Among them, motifs I and V bind to the SMC2 neck and the SMC4 cap regions, respectively (Hassler et al., 2019), whereas motifs II and IV interact with CAP-D2 and CAP-G, respectively (Piazza et al., 2014; Kschonsak et al., 2017; Hara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Piazza et al., 2014; Kschonsak et al., 2017; Hara et al., 2019.

claim: Motif IV of CAP-H interacts with CAP-G.
source: Among them, motifs I and V bind to the SMC2 neck and the SMC4 cap regions, respectively (Hassler et al., 2019), whereas motifs II and IV interact with CAP-D2 and CAP-G, respectively (Piazza et al., 2014; Kschonsak et al., 2017; Hara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Piazza et al., 2014; Kschonsak et al., 2017; Hara et al., 2019.

claim: The CAP-H N-tail is ~80 amino-acid long in vertebrates.
source: This extension, the CAP-H N-tail, has several characteristic features as summarized below. Firstly, it is ~80 amino-acid long in vertebrates, but the corresponding extension is much shorter or completely missing in fungi (Bazile et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bazile et al., 2010 and sequence analysis.

claim: The N-terminal extension corresponding to the CAP-H N-tail is much shorter or completely missing in fungi.
source: This extension, the CAP-H N-tail, has several characteristic features as summarized below. Firstly, it is ~80 amino-acid long in vertebrates, but the corresponding extension is much shorter or completely missing in fungi (Bazile et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bazile et al., 2010.

claim: Most of the CAP-H N-tail is predicted to be structurally disordered.
source: Secondly, although most of the N-tail is predicted to be structurally disordered, a stretch of ~17-amino-acid long, located in its middle region, is conserved among vertebrates and is predicted to form an α-helix, as judged by both the conventional secondary structure prediction software Jpred4 (https://www.compbio.dundee.ac.uk/jpred/) and AlphaFold2 (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/).
evidence: This claim is based on computational predictions using Jpred4 and AlphaFold2.

claim: A stretch of ~17-amino-acid long in the middle region of the CAP-H N-tail is conserved among vertebrates and is predicted to form an α-helix.
source: Secondly, although most of the N-tail is predicted to be structurally disordered, a stretch of ~17-amino-acid long, located in its middle region, is conserved among vertebrates and is predicted to form an α-helix, as judged by both the conventional secondary structure prediction software Jpred4 (https://www.compbio.dundee.ac.uk/jpred/) and AlphaFold2 (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/).
evidence: This claim is based on computational predictions using Jpred4 and AlphaFold2.

claim: The vertebrate CAP-H N-tail contains multiple SP/TP sites.
source: Thirdly, the vertebrate N-tail contains multiple SP/TP sites, sites often targeted by cyclin–CDK complexes, although their number varies among different species.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and knowledge of CDK phosphorylation sites.

claim: SP/TP sites are often targeted by cyclin–CDK complexes.
source: Thirdly, the vertebrate N-tail contains multiple SP/TP sites, sites often targeted by cyclin–CDK complexes, although their number varies among different species.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CDK phosphorylation specificity.

claim: Significantly higher levels of holo(H-dN) were detected on chromatin than holo(WT) at both 30 and 150 min time points.
source: Remarkably, we found that significantly higher levels of holo(H-dN) were detected on chromatin than holo(WT) at both time points and at the different concentrations of condensin I tested (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Chromosomes assembled with 35 nM holo(H-dN) at 150 min were much thinner than those assembled with 35 nM holo(WT) at 150 min.
source: It was also noticed that the chromosomes assembled with 35 nM holo(H-dN) at 150 min were much thinner than those assembled with 35 nM holo(WT) at 150 min (Figure 1B, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, D.

claim: Chromosomes assembled with 17.5 nM holo(H-dN) were comparable with those assembled with 35 nM holo(WT) in terms of both morphology and mSMC4 signal levels.
source: When the concentration of holo(H-dN) was reduced to 17.5 nM, the resultant chromosomes were comparable with those assembled with 35 nM holo(WT), in terms of both the morphology and the mSMC4 signal levels (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: The chromosomal levels of condensin I are tightly correlated with the chromosome morphology produced.
source: Taken together, we concluded that the deletion of the CAP-H N-tail accelerates the loading of condensin I on chromosomes in M-HSS, and that the chromosomal levels of condensin I are tightly correlated with the chromosome morphology produced.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing dose-dependent effects.

claim: Holo(H-dCH) exhibited a phenotype very similar to that of holo(H-dN) in terms of both increased condensin I loading and resultant chromosome morphology.
source: We found that the holo(H-dCH) and holo(H-crCH) exhibited a phenotype very similar to that of holo(H-dN) in terms of both increased condensin I loading and resultant chromosome morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Holo(H-crCH) exhibited a phenotype very similar to that of holo(H-dN) in terms of both increased condensin I loading and resultant chromosome morphology.
source: We found that the holo(H-dCH) and holo(H-crCH) exhibited a phenotype very similar to that of holo(H-dN) in terms of both increased condensin I loading and resultant chromosome morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The conserved helix and its positive charges play an important role in negatively regulating condensin I loading in M-HSS.
source: Thus, the CH and its positive charges play an important role in negatively regulating condensin I loading in M-HSS.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data with H-dCH and H-crCH mutants.

claim: Xenopus CAP-H is phosphorylated in a mitosis-specific manner in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Previous studies had shown that Xenopus CAP-H is phosphorylated in a mitosis-specific manner in Xenopus egg extracts (Hirano et al., 1997; Kimura et al., 1998), and that Xenopus and human CAP-H can be phosphorylated by cyclin B-Cdk1 in vitro (Kimura et al., 1998; Kimura et al., 2001; Shintomi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hirano et al., 1997 and Kimura et al., 1998.

claim: Xenopus and human CAP-H can be phosphorylated by cyclin B-Cdk1 in vitro.
source: Previous studies had shown that Xenopus CAP-H is phosphorylated in a mitosis-specific manner in Xenopus egg extracts (Hirano et al., 1997; Kimura et al., 1998), and that Xenopus and human CAP-H can be phosphorylated by cyclin B-Cdk1 in vitro (Kimura et al., 1998; Kimura et al., 2001; Shintomi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kimura et al., 1998; Kimura et al., 2001; Shintomi et al., 2015.

claim: hCAP-H has three SP sites and one TP site in its N-tail.
source: Whereas hCAP-H has three SP sites and one TP site in its N-tail (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), it is known that Cdk1 phosphorylation is not exclusively proline directed (Brown et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2015; Krasinska and Fisher, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cdk1 phosphorylation is not exclusively proline directed.
source: Whereas hCAP-H has three SP sites and one TP site in its N-tail (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), it is known that Cdk1 phosphorylation is not exclusively proline directed (Brown et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2015; Krasinska and Fisher, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2015; Krasinska and Fisher, 2022.

claim: Two phosphoepitopes (pS17 and pS76) were detectable in holo(WT) but not in holo(H-N19A) when incubated with M-HSS.
source: When the holo(WT) and holo(H-N19A) were incubated with M-HSS, two phosphoepitopes (pS17 and pS76) were detectable in the former, but not in the latter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Neither pS17 nor pS76 epitopes were detected in both holo(WT) and holo(H-N19A) that had been incubated with interphase HSS.
source: Neither of the epitopes was detected in both complexes that had been incubated with interphase HSS (I-HSS), indicating that the corresponding sites are phosphorylated in holo(WT) in a mitosis-specific manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and indicates mitosis-specific phosphorylation.

claim: The pS17 and pS76 sites are phosphorylated in holo(WT) in a mitosis-specific manner.
source: Neither of the epitopes was detected in both complexes that had been incubated with interphase HSS (I-HSS), indicating that the corresponding sites are phosphorylated in holo(WT) in a mitosis-specific manner.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential phosphorylation in M-HSS versus I-HSS.

claim: The loading of holo(H-N19A) onto chromatin was greatly reduced compared to holo(WT) or holo(H-dN).
source: We found that the loading of holo(H-N19A) onto chromatin was greatly reduced compared to holo(WT) or holo(H-dN) (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Chromosomes produced by holo(H-N19A) were poorly organized and abnormally thick, having hazy surfaces.
source: The resultant chromosomes produced by holo(H-N19A) were poorly organized and abnormally thick, having hazy surfaces (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Holo(H-N19D) behaved very similarly to holo(H-dN) in the add-back assay.
source: Remarkably, we found that holo(H-N19D) behaved very similarly to holo(H-dN) in the add-back assay (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D–F.

claim: Multisite phosphorylation in the CAP-H N-tail relieves its negative effects on condensin I loading and mitotic chromosome assembly.
source: Although we cannot rule out the possibility that the introduction of multiple mutations into the N-tail causes unforeseeable adverse effects on protein conformations, these results supported the idea that multisite phosphorylation in the CAP-H N-tail relieves its negative effects on condensin I loading and mitotic chromosome assembly.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the comparison of phosphorylation-deficient and phosphorylation-mimetic mutants.

claim: Endogenous Xenopus condensins failed to associate with chromatin in I-HSS.
source: Consistent with the previous study (Hirano et al., 1997), endogenous Xenopus condensins failed to associate with chromatin in I-HSS, leaving a spherical compact mass, although they bound to chromatin and assembled a cluster of rod-shaped chromosomes in M-HSS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Hirano et al., 1997.

claim: Endogenous Xenopus condensins bound to chromatin and assembled a cluster of rod-shaped chromosomes in M-HSS.
source: Consistent with the previous study (Hirano et al., 1997), endogenous Xenopus condensins failed to associate with chromatin in I-HSS, leaving a spherical compact mass, although they bound to chromatin and assembled a cluster of rod-shaped chromosomes in M-HSS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sperm nuclei in condensin-depleted I-HSS were transiently swollen at early time points (15–30 min) and then converted into compact chromatin masses at a late time point (150 min).
source: We found that the nuclei were transiently swollen at early time points (15–30 min) and then converted into compact chromatin masses at a late time point (150 min) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Significant levels of mSMC4 signals were detectable on chromatin when condensin-depleted extract was supplemented with 35 nM holo(H-dN), especially at early time points.
source: When the condensin-depleted extract was supplemented with 35 nM holo(H-dN), however, significant levels of mSMC4 signals were detectable on chromatin, especially at early time points (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 150 nM holo(WT) produced a temporal series of chromatin masses that was very similar to that observed with 35 nM holo(H-dN).
source: We found that 150 nM holo(WT) produced a temporal series of chromatin masses that was very similar to that observed with 35 nM holo(H-dN).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different concentrations.

claim: 150 nM holo(H-dN) produced a cluster of rod-shaped, mitotic chromosome-like structures with mSMC4-positive axes at 150 min in I-HSS.
source: At 150 min, although mSMC4 signals on chromatin decreased, a cluster of rod-shaped, mitotic chromosome-like structures with mSMC4-positive axes was clearly discernible in each of the chromatin masses (Figure 3B, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, D.

claim: Not only the SP/TP sites in the CAP-H N-tail but also those in the CAP-D2 C-tail were barely phosphorylated in I-HSS.
source: It is important to note that not only the SP/TP sites in the CAP-H N-tail but also those in the CAP-D2 C-tail were barely phosphorylated in I-HSS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Holo(H-crCH) behaved similarly to holo(H-dN) in the add-back assay at 150 nM in I-HSS.
source: We found that both mutant complexes behaved similarly to holo(H-dN) although the loading efficiency of holo(H-N19D) was somewhat lower than that of holo(H-crCH).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The loading efficiency of holo(H-N19D) was somewhat lower than that of holo(H-crCH) in I-HSS.
source: We found that both mutant complexes behaved similarly to holo(H-dN) although the loading efficiency of holo(H-N19D) was somewhat lower than that of holo(H-crCH).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: When the CAP-H N-tail is compromised, condensin I gains the ability to assemble mitotic chromosome-like structures even in interphase extracts.
source: These results demonstrated that, when the CAP-H N-tail is compromised, condensin I gains the ability to assemble mitotic chromosome-like structures even in interphase extracts.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data with multiple N-tail mutants in I-HSS.

claim: A significantly higher amount (~2.5-fold) of nicked circular DNA was recovered with holo(H-dN) than with holo(WT) in the topological loading assay.
source: Notably, a significantly higher amount (~2.5-fold) of nicked circular DNA was recovered with holo(H-dN) than with holo(WT) (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: Virtually no linear DNA was recovered with either holo(WT) or holo(H-dN) regardless of the presence or absence of nucleotides in the topological loading assay.
source: Under this condition, virtually no linear DNA was recovered with either holo(WT) or holo(H-dN) regardless of the presence or absence of nucleotides (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Nicked circular DNA was recovered on the beads with holo(WT) in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: In contrast, nicked circular DNA was recovered on the beads with holo(WT) in an ATP-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Holo(WT) and holo(H-dN) formed DNA loops on ~17% and ~33% of the U-shaped DNA, respectively, in the presence of ATP.
source: We found that holo(WT) and holo(H-dN) formed DNA loops on ~17% and ~33% of the U-shaped DNA, respectively, in the presence of ATP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No significant differences were observed between holo(WT) and holo(H-dN) in the rate of loop extrusion, the loop duration time, or the loop size formed.
source: Despite the difference in the frequency of loop formation, no significant differences were observed between holo(WT) and holo(H-dN) in other parameters, such as the rate of loop extrusion, the loop duration time, or the loop size formed (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: Neither holo(WT) nor holo(H-dN) supported loop formation in the absence of ATP.
source: Neither holo(WT) nor holo(H-dN) supported loop formation in the absence of ATP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of the CAP-H N-tail affects the initial interactions with DNA, but not the core activity responsible for the expansion of DNA loops.
source: Taken together, these results show that deletion of the CAP-H N-tail affects the initial interactions with DNA, but not the core activity responsible for the expansion of DNA loops.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the topological loading and loop extrusion assay results.

claim: Mitotic phosphorylation of Cut3/SMC4 regulates the nuclear import of condensin in fission yeast.
source: Previous studies showed that mitotic phosphorylation of Cut3/SMC4 regulates the nuclear import of condensin in fission yeast (Sutani et al., 1999) and that phosphorylation of Smc4/SMC4 slows down the dynamic turnover of condensin on mitotic chromosomes in budding yeast (Robellet et al., 2015; Thadani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sutani et al., 1999.

claim: Phosphorylation of Smc4/SMC4 slows down the dynamic turnover of condensin on mitotic chromosomes in budding yeast.
source: Previous studies showed that mitotic phosphorylation of Cut3/SMC4 regulates the nuclear import of condensin in fission yeast (Sutani et al., 1999) and that phosphorylation of Smc4/SMC4 slows down the dynamic turnover of condensin on mitotic chromosomes in budding yeast (Robellet et al., 2015; Thadani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Robellet et al., 2015 and Thadani et al., 2018.

claim: Deletion of the CAP-D2 C-tail has little impact on condensin I function as judged by add-back assays using Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Recent studies from our laboratory showed that deletion of the CAP-D2 C-tail, which also contains multiple SP/TP sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), has little impact on condensin I function as judged by the same and related add-back assays using Xenopus egg extracts (Kinoshita et al., 2022; Yoshida et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kinoshita et al., 2022 and Yoshida et al., 2022.

claim: The CAP-H N-tail represents the first example of negative regulatory elements that have been identified in vertebrate condensin I.
source: Thus, the CAP-H N-tail represents the first example of negative regulatory elements that have been identified in vertebrate condensin I.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the current study's findings and comparison with previous work.

claim: The SMC2-kleisin gate is closed when the CAP-H motif I binds to the SMC2 and prevents its untimely opening during interphase.
source: The SMC2-kleisin gate is closed when the CAP-H motif I binds to the SMC2 (Hassler et al., 2019) and prevents its untimely opening during interphase.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the current study's findings and citation to Hassler et al., 2019.

claim: The conserved helix located in the middle of the N-tail could play a critical contribution to stabilization of the closed SMC2-kleisin gate.
source: The CH located in the middle of the N-tail could play a critical contribution to this stabilization.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Upon mitotic entry, multisite phosphorylation of the N-tail relieves the stabilization, allowing the opening of the DNA entry gate.
source: Upon mitotic entry, multisite phosphorylation of the N-tail relieves the stabilization, allowing the opening of the DNA entry gate, hence, the loading of condensin I onto chromosomes.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the current study's findings.

claim: The kleisin N-tail of vertebrate condensin I could act as a 'gatekeeper' of the SMC2-kleisin gate.
source: Thus, the kleisin N-tail of vertebrate condensin I could act as a 'gatekeeper' of the SMC2-kleisin gate.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the proposed model.

claim: Multisite phosphorylation of the CAP-H N-tail may set up an ultrasensitive switch-like response that can be activated at a certain threshold level of phosphorylation.
source: It is possible that, analogous to the Cdk1 inhibitor Sic1 (Örd et al., 2019), multisite phosphorylation of the CAP-H N-tail sets up an ultrasensitive switch-like response that can be activated at a certain threshold level of phosphorylation, thereby ensuring robust cell cycle regulation of condensin I loading.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on analogy to Sic1 and citation to Örd et al., 2019.

claim: CAP-H2, the kleisin subunit of condensin II, lacks the N-terminal extension that corresponds to the CAP-H N-tail.
source: It should be added that CAP-H2, the kleisin subunit of condensin II, lacks the N-terminal extension that corresponds to the CAP-H N-tail.
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence analysis and knowledge of condensin II structure.

claim: The negative regulation by the kleisin N-tail is not shared by condensin II.
source: Thus, the negative regulation by the kleisin N-tail reported here is not shared by condensin II.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the absence of the N-tail in CAP-H2.

claim: Deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail causes accelerated loading of condensin II onto chromatin.
source: Interestingly, however, a recent study from our laboratory has shown that the deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail causes accelerated loading of condensin II onto chromatin (Yoshida et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2022.

claim: Condensins I and II may utilize similar IDR-mediated regulatory mechanisms, but they do so in different ways.
source: It is therefore possible that condensins I and II utilize similar IDR-mediated regulatory mechanisms, but they do so in different ways.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on comparison of condensins I and II regulation.

claim: Aurora B is not essential for single chromatid assembly in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Accumulating, multiple lines of evidence, however, strongly argue against this model: (1) aurora B is not essential for single chromatid assembly in Xenopus egg extracts (MacCallum et al., 2002) or in a reconstitution assay (Shintomi et al., 2015); (2) the H2A N-tail is dispensable for condensin I-dependent chromatid assembly in the reconstitution assay (Shintomi et al., 2015); (3) even whole nucleosomes are not essential for condensin I-mediated assembly of chromatid-like structures (Shintomi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MacCallum et al., 2002 and Shintomi et al., 2015.

claim: Condensin I was phosphorylated in a mitosis-specific manner in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Early studies demonstrated that condensin I is phosphorylated in a mitosis-specific manner in Xenopus egg extracts (Hirano et al., 1997), and that the positive supercoiling activity of condensin I can be activated by Cdk1 phosphorylation in vitro (Kimura et al., 1998; Kimura et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hirano et al., 1997.
